## 1. Load data and align reviewer_id / book_id

`book_id_mapping.csv` was produced by `match_book_ids.py`, which matched
every one of the 50,000 annotated reviews to
`goodreads_reviews_dedup.json` on **user_id = Reviewer ID** and
**identical (whitespace-normalised) review text**.

```{r}
ROOT <- "C:/Users/gujia/Downloads/independent-capstone-project/Naive_LLM_analysis"   # project root; every path below is relative to it
setwd(ROOT)
if (isTRUE(getOption("knitr.in.progress"))) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = ROOT)  # keep ROOT for later chunks

library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

df  <- read.csv("data/annotated/annotated_50000sample.csv", check.names = FALSE,
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
map <- read.csv("data/book_id_mapping/book_id_mapping.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                colClasses = c(book_id = "character", review_id = "character"))

df$row         <- seq_len(nrow(df)) - 1      # 0-based row index used by the Python script
df             <- merge(df, map, by = "row", all.x = TRUE, sort = TRUE)
df$reviewer_id <- df[["Reviewer ID"]]

table(df$match_type, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r}
# keep reviews that were aligned to a book_id
df <- df[!is.na(df$book_id) & df$book_id != "", ]

c(reviews   = nrow(df),
  reviewers = length(unique(df$reviewer_id)),
  books     = length(unique(df$book_id)))

# how clustered is the data?
summary(as.vector(table(df$reviewer_id)))   # reviews per reviewer
summary(as.vector(table(df$book_id)))       # reviews per book
```

## 2. Split Genre into combinations

Each `;`-separated piece of the Genre cell is one combination, e.g.
`"fantasy, paranormal; fiction"` → `"fantasy, paranormal"` and
`"fiction"`.

```{r}
genre_list <- lapply(strsplit(df$Genre, ";"), trimws)
genre_list <- lapply(genre_list, function(x) x[x != ""])
combos <- sort(unique(unlist(genre_list)))

# syntactic variable names: "fantasy, paranormal" -> "fantasy_paranormal"
clean_name <- function(x) gsub("_+", "_", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", x))
data.frame(combination = combos, variable = clean_name(combos))
```

## 3. One-hot encoding

1 = the book has this combination, 0 = it does not.

```{r}
for (cmb in combos) {
  df[[clean_name(cmb)]] <- as.integer(vapply(genre_list, function(g) cmb %in% g, logical(1)))
}

# rename outcome columns: "Absence of Naive Realism_AI" -> "Absence_of_Naive_Realism_AI"
ai_cols <- grep("_AI$", names(df), value = TRUE)
names(df)[match(ai_cols, names(df))] <- clean_name(ai_cols)

df$reviewer_id <- factor(df$reviewer_id)
df$book_id     <- factor(df$book_id)

# number of reviews per combination
colSums(df[clean_name(combos)])

write.csv(df, "data/analysis_ready/annotated_50000sample_onehot_ids.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
```

## 4. Random-intercept logistic models

$$
\operatorname{logit} P(Y_{ijk}=1) = \beta_0 + \sum_{g}\beta_g\,\text{Genre}_{g,k} + u_{j} + v_{k},
\qquad u_j \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\text{reviewer}}),\; v_k \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\text{book}})
$$

for review *i* written by reviewer *j* about book *k*. The two random
intercepts absorb the non-independence of reviews written by the same
reviewer and reviews of the same book.

```{r}
ctrl <- glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))

# nAGQ = 0: fast approximation used for the main results (nAGQ = 1 = Laplace, compared in Section 8)
NAGQ <- 0
dir.create("cache/models_nagq0", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Fit a model, or load it if it was already fitted (fit_glmm_parallel.R fits all 7 in parallel).
# For nAGQ = 1 the nAGQ = 0 estimates are used as starting values.
fit_glmm <- function(name, formula, nAGQ = NAGQ) {
  path <- if (nAGQ == 0) sprintf("cache/models_nagq0/%s_nagq0.rds", name) else
    sprintf("cache/models_nagq1/%s_nagq%d.rds", name, nAGQ)
  if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  start <- NULL
  path0 <- sprintf("cache/models_nagq0/%s_nagq0.rds", name)
  if (nAGQ > 0 && file.exists(path0)) {
    m0 <- readRDS(path0)
    start <- list(theta = getME(m0, "theta"), fixef = fixef(m0))
  }
  m <- glmer(formula, data = df, family = binomial, control = ctrl, nAGQ = nAGQ, start = start)
  saveRDS(m, path)
  m
}
```

## 5. Tables

Fixed effects are reported on the log-odds scale and as odds ratios (OR)
with Wald 95% CIs. OR \> 1: reviews of books with this genre combination
are more likely to be coded 1.

```{r}
make_table <- function(model, outcome) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(model)))
  names(ct) <- c("log_odds", "std_error", "z_value", "p_value")
  ct$term     <- rownames(ct)
  ct$OR       <- exp(ct$log_odds)
  ct$OR_lower <- exp(ct$log_odds - 1.96 * ct$std_error)
  ct$OR_upper <- exp(ct$log_odds + 1.96 * ct$std_error)
  ct$sig <- as.character(cut(ct$p_value, breaks = c(-Inf, .001, .01, .05, Inf),
                             labels = c("***", "**", "*", "")))
  ct$outcome <- outcome
  ct$n <- nobs(model)
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
  ct[, c("outcome", "term", "log_odds", "std_error", "z_value", "p_value", "sig",
         "OR", "OR_lower", "OR_upper", "n")]
}

make_re_table <- function(model, outcome) {
  vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
  v_rev  <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "reviewer_id"]
  v_book <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "book_id"]
  total  <- v_rev + v_book + pi^2 / 3          # latent-scale residual variance of logit
  data.frame(outcome = outcome,
             var_reviewer = v_rev, var_book = v_book,
             ICC_reviewer = v_rev / total, ICC_book = v_book / total)
}
```

```{r}
res_g1 <- make_table(g1, "Absence_of_Naive_Realism")
knitr::kable(res_g1, digits = 4)
```

## 6. Graphs

```{r}
genre_vars <- c("children", "comics_graphic", "fantasy_paranormal", "fiction",
                "history_historical_fiction_biography", "mystery_thriller_crime",
                "non_fiction", "poetry", "romance", "young_adult")

genre_labels <- c("Children", "Comics & Graphic", "Fantasy & Paranormal", "Fiction",
                  "History / Biography", "Mystery / Thriller / Crime", "Non-fiction",
                  "Poetry", "Romance", "Young Adult")

make_plot_data <- function(res) {
  res %>%
    filter(term %in% genre_vars) %>%
    mutate(significance = ifelse(sig == "", "ns", sig),
           term = factor(term, levels = genre_vars, labels = genre_labels))
}

plot_or <- function(res, title) {
  ggplot(make_plot_data(res), aes(x = OR, y = term)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = OR_lower, xmax = OR_upper), width = 0.2, orientation = "y") +
    geom_point(aes(color = significance), size = 3) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("***" = "#B2182B", "**" = "#EF8A62",
                                  "*" = "#67A9CF", "ns" = "gray65"),
                       drop = FALSE) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = paste0("Random intercepts for reviewer and book (nAGQ = ", NAGQ, ")"),
         x = "Odds Ratio (log scale, 95% CI)", y = "Genre Combination",
         color = "Significance") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
          legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

## 7. Summary

### 7.1 Data alignment

```{r}
mt <- table(read.csv("data/book_id_mapping/book_id_mapping.csv")$match_type)
n_rev  <- length(unique(df$reviewer_id))
n_book <- length(unique(df$book_id))
```

-   Of the 50,000 annotated reviews,
    **`r format(nrow(df), big.mark=",")`** were aligned to a Goodreads
    `book_id` via `goodreads_reviews_dedup.json`
    (`r round(100*nrow(df)/50000, 1)`%).
    `r format(sum(mt[c("exact_text","exact_text+rating")]), big.mark=",")`
    matched on identical text, `r format(mt["prefix200"], big.mark=",")`
    on the first 200 characters, and
    `r format(mt["fuzzy_text>=0.9"], big.mark=",")` by fuzzy text
    similarity (≥ 0.90) within the same reviewer, rating and genre set.
    For every matched review the raw rating equals the star rating and
    the book's genre set equals the Genre cell, which confirms the
    alignment.
-   `r sum(mt[c("ambiguous","unmatched")])` reviews could not be aligned
    uniquely (the same reviewer posted identical text for several books,
    or no match) and are excluded.
-   The analysed data contain **`r format(n_rev, big.mark=",")`
    reviewers** and **`r format(n_book, big.mark=",")` books**.

### 7.2 Clustering: who writes the review vs. which book is reviewed

```{r}
re_show <- re_all
re_show$ICC_total <- re_show$ICC_reviewer + re_show$ICC_book
knitr::kable(re_show[, c("outcome", "var_reviewer", "var_book", "ICC_reviewer", "ICC_book", "ICC_total")],
             digits = 3, col.names = c("Construct", "Var reviewer", "Var book",
                                       "ICC reviewer", "ICC book", "ICC total"))
```

- **Non-independence is substantial for every construct.** Reviewer and book together account for
  roughly 11% (Surprise) to 26% (Critic, Thought-Provoking, Change) of the latent variance. Treating the
  49,823 reviews as independent, as the OLS t-tests did, therefore overstates precision.
- **The source of clustering differs by construct, which is substantively informative:**
    - *Reviewer-driven* constructs: **Critic** (ICC reviewer = .23 vs. book = .03), **Theme** (.19 vs. .05)
      and **Absence of Naive Realism** (.15 vs. .05). Whether a review offers reasoned evaluation,
      interprets meaning, or acknowledges other viewpoints is largely a stable *writing style* of the
      reviewer, not a property of the book.
    - *Book-driven* constructs: **Change** (book = .20 vs. reviewer = .07) and **Thought-Provoking**
      (.18 vs. .08). Whether a review reports being made to think or having its author's views changed
      depends more on *which book* was read.
    - **Ease** is split fairly evenly (.11 vs. .09); **Surprise** shows the least clustering of either kind.

### 7.3 Genre effects by construct

Odds ratios from the random-intercept models (\*p < .05, \*\*p < .01, \*\*\*p < .001):

```{r}
or_wide <- res_all[res_all$term %in% genre_vars, ]
or_wide$cell <- sprintf("%.2f%s", or_wide$OR, or_wide$sig)
or_wide <- reshape(or_wide[, c("term", "outcome", "cell")], idvar = "term",
                   timevar = "outcome", direction = "wide")
names(or_wide) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(or_wide))
or_wide$term <- genre_labels[match(or_wide$term, genre_vars)]
knitr::kable(or_wide, row.names = FALSE)
```

53 of the 70 genre coefficients are significant at p < .05. Read by genre, they form clear profiles:

- **Non-fiction: the strongest "reflective" profile.** Non-fiction reviews have almost three times the
  odds of reporting a change in views (**Change** OR = 2.90\*\*\*), and much higher odds of being
  **Thought-Provoking** (2.29\*\*\*), discussing **Theme** (1.80\*\*\*) and showing **Absence of Naive
  Realism** (1.38\*\*\*). They are, however, *less* likely to contain craft-oriented **Critic** evaluation
  (0.72\*\*\*). Ease and Surprise do not differ.
- **Poetry: similar but weaker.** Higher odds of **Thought-Provoking** (1.83\*\*\*), **Theme** (1.32\*)
  and **Absence of Naive Realism** (1.31\*), lower odds of **Critic** (0.72\*\*). Poetry is the smallest
  category (about 500 reviews), so its intervals are wide.
- **Young Adult: consistently positive.** Higher odds on six of seven constructs: **Change** (1.46\*\*\*),
  **Thought-Provoking** (1.35\*\*\*), **Theme** (1.18\*\*\*), **Surprise** (1.16\*\*\*), **Absence of
  Naive Realism** (1.15\*\*\*) and **Critic** (1.10\*\*\*); only **Ease** is slightly lower (0.94\*).
- **History / Biography: modestly reflective.** Higher **Theme** (1.17\*\*\*), **Absence of Naive
  Realism** (1.14\*\*\*), **Critic** (1.09\*\*) and **Thought-Provoking** (1.09\*); lower **Ease** (0.92\*\*).
- **Romance: easy, but less reflective.** The highest-ease adult genre (**Ease** 1.24\*\*\*), but about
  half the odds of **Thought-Provoking** (0.51\*\*\*) and **Change** (0.51\*\*\*), and lower **Theme**
  (0.68\*\*\*) and **Absence of Naive Realism** (0.72\*\*\*). Critic and Surprise do not differ.
- **Children and Comics & Graphic: easy, but lower on everything else.** These are the two genres with the
  highest **Ease** (1.47\*\*\* and 1.38\*\*\*), and they are significantly *lower* on all six other
  constructs (ORs between 0.61 and 0.87).
- **Mystery / Thriller / Crime: surprise and critique.** Higher **Surprise** (1.19\*\*\*) and **Critic**
  (1.19\*\*\*), consistent with plot-twist-driven reading, but lower **Change** (0.69\*\*\*) and **Theme**
  (0.89\*\*\*).
- **Fantasy & Paranormal: slightly less reflective.** Lower **Change** (0.56\*\*\*), **Thought-Provoking**
  (0.72\*\*\*), **Theme** (0.91\*\*\*), **Absence of Naive Realism** (0.89\*\*\*) and **Ease** (0.93\*\*);
  marginally higher **Critic** (1.08\*\*) and **Surprise** (1.06\*).
- **Fiction** applies to about 98% of books, so its effect is weakly identified; it is significant only for
  **Absence of Naive Realism** (1.26\*) and **Theme** (1.26\*\*).

### 7.4 Patterns across constructs

```{r}
genre_only <- res_all[res_all$term %in% genre_vars, ]
cross <- data.frame(
  genre        = genre_labels,
  n_sig_up     = sapply(genre_vars, function(g) sum(genre_only$term == g & genre_only$p_value < .05 & genre_only$OR > 1)),
  n_sig_down   = sapply(genre_vars, function(g) sum(genre_only$term == g & genre_only$p_value < .05 & genre_only$OR < 1)),
  n_ns         = sapply(genre_vars, function(g) sum(genre_only$term == g & genre_only$p_value >= .05)),
  row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(cross, col.names = c("Genre combination", "# constructs higher (p<.05)",
                                  "# constructs lower (p<.05)", "# not significant"))
```

1. **An ease-reflection trade-off.** The genres that make reading feel easiest (Children, Comics &
   Graphic, Romance) are the ones whose reviews are least likely to be thought-provoking, thematic or
   view-changing. Non-fiction and Poetry show the reverse pattern. At the genre level, Ease behaves almost
   as a mirror image of the reflective constructs.
2. **Change and Thought-Provoking are the most genre-sensitive constructs** (widest OR range, 0.51 to
   2.90), consistent with their book-level ICCs being the largest: these experiences depend on *what* is
   read.
3. **Critic follows a different logic.** It is higher for plot-driven genres (Mystery 1.19, Young Adult
   1.10, Fantasy 1.08) and lower for Non-fiction, Poetry and Children, and its clustering is almost
   entirely at the reviewer level. Critical evaluation appears to be more a property of the reviewer and
   of narrative genres than of intellectually demanding content.
4. **Surprise is the least genre-dependent construct** (5 significant effects, the lowest ICCs), and is
   mainly elevated for Mystery / Thriller / Crime and Young Adult.

### 7.5 Comparison with the OLS models (`genre_lm_ttests.qmd`)

- After accounting for reviewer and book, **53 of 70** genre effects remain significant, compared with
  56 in OLS. All 53 GLMM-significant effects were also significant in OLS, and the direction of the
  effect agrees for 69 of 70 coefficients. The one disagreement (Poetry on Change) is null in both models.
- Three effects lose significance in the nAGQ = 0 models: **Fiction on Thought-Provoking**
  (OLS p = .002, GLMM p = .064), **Mystery / Thriller / Crime on Thought-Provoking** (p < .001, GLMM
  p = .057) and **Romance on Critic** (p < .001, GLMM p = .099). With the more accurate Laplace fit
  (nAGQ = 1, Section 8) all three return to p < .05 (p = .028, .034, .034). They are therefore
  **borderline effects whose significance depends on the estimation method** and should be reported
  with caution rather than as clear differences.
- The substantive conclusions are therefore robust; modelling non-independence mainly corrects the
  over-precision of the OLS estimates.

### 7.6 Interpretation notes

-   Genre is a **book-level** variable, so its effects are estimated
    mainly from differences *between books*; the book random intercept
    captures remaining book-to-book differences not explained by genre.
-   Each OR compares books **with** a genre combination to books
    **without** it, holding the other nine combinations constant. The
    intercept (a book with none of the ten combinations) does not occur
    in the data and should not be interpreted.
-   Odds ratios are conditional (reviewer- and book-specific) effects,
    so they are typically larger in magnitude than population-averaged
    effects from the OLS models in `genre_lm_ttests.qmd`.
-   Change (≈3% coded 1) and Absence of Naive Realism (≈14%) are rare
    outcomes; their CIs are wider, especially for small genres such as
    Poetry (n ≈ 500) and Non-fiction (n ≈ 1,700).
-   Outcomes are GPT-4o codes (v1 prompts), so effects describe how the
    AI coder labels reviews; any systematic coder error that correlates
    with genre would also appear here.

## 8. Robustness: nAGQ = 0 vs nAGQ = 1 (Laplace)

The main results use `nAGQ = 0`, which estimates the fixed effects inside the penalised
iteratively re-weighted least-squares step (fast). `nAGQ = 1` (Laplace approximation) optimises the
fixed effects and variance components jointly on the approximate likelihood (slow, more accurate).
The nAGQ = 1 models were fitted with the nAGQ = 0 estimates as starting values.

```{r}
have_nagq1 <- all(file.exists(sprintf("cache/models_nagq1/g%d_nagq1.rds", 1:7)))
have_nagq1
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_nagq1
outcome_names <- c("Absence_of_Naive_Realism", "Theme", "Thought_Provoking", "Ease",
                   "Critic", "Surprise", "Change")
m1_list <- lapply(1:7, function(k) readRDS(sprintf("cache/models_nagq1/g%d_nagq1.rds", k)))

res_all_1 <- do.call(rbind, Map(make_table, m1_list, outcome_names))
re_all_1  <- do.call(rbind, Map(make_re_table, m1_list, outcome_names))
write.csv(res_all_1, "results/GLMM_nAGQ1/genre_glmer_coefficients_nagq1.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(re_all_1,  "results/GLMM_nAGQ1/genre_glmer_random_effects_nagq1.csv", row.names = FALSE)

cmp <- merge(res_all[, c("outcome", "term", "log_odds", "std_error", "p_value", "sig")],
             res_all_1[, c("outcome", "term", "log_odds", "std_error", "p_value", "sig")],
             by = c("outcome", "term"), suffixes = c("_q0", "_q1"))
cmp <- cmp[cmp$term %in% genre_vars, ]
cmp$diff_log_odds <- cmp$log_odds_q1 - cmp$log_odds_q0
cmp$same_sig_at_05 <- (cmp$p_value_q0 < .05) == (cmp$p_value_q1 < .05)
cmp$same_sign <- sign(cmp$log_odds_q0) == sign(cmp$log_odds_q1)
cmp$outcome <- factor(cmp$outcome, levels = outcome_names)
cmp <- cmp[order(cmp$outcome, cmp$term), ]
knitr::kable(cmp, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_nagq1
re_cmp <- merge(re_all, re_all_1, by = "outcome", suffixes = c("_q0", "_q1"))
re_cmp <- re_cmp[match(outcome_names, re_cmp$outcome),
                 c("outcome", "var_reviewer_q0", "var_reviewer_q1", "var_book_q0", "var_book_q1",
                   "ICC_reviewer_q0", "ICC_reviewer_q1", "ICC_book_q0", "ICC_book_q1")]
knitr::kable(re_cmp, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

fit_cmp <- data.frame(
  outcome = outcome_names,
  logLik_q0 = sapply(list(g1, g2, g3, g4, g5, g6, g7), function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m))),
  logLik_q1 = sapply(m1_list, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m))),
  converged_q1 = sapply(m1_list, function(m) is.null(m@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages)))
knitr::kable(fit_cmp, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_nagq1
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 7
ggplot(cmp, aes(x = log_odds_q0, y = log_odds_q1, color = outcome)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Genre coefficients: nAGQ = 0 vs nAGQ = 1",
       x = "log-odds, nAGQ = 0", y = "log-odds, nAGQ = 1", color = "Construct") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_nagq1
#| results: asis
cat(sprintf("- Correlation of the %d genre coefficients across the two methods: r = %.4f.\n",
            nrow(cmp), cor(cmp$log_odds_q0, cmp$log_odds_q1)))
cat(sprintf("- Largest absolute difference in log-odds: %.3f (%s, %s).\n",
            max(abs(cmp$diff_log_odds)), cmp$term[which.max(abs(cmp$diff_log_odds))],
            cmp$outcome[which.max(abs(cmp$diff_log_odds))]))
cat(sprintf("- Same sign: %d / %d; same significance decision at p < .05: %d / %d.\n",
            sum(cmp$same_sign), nrow(cmp), sum(cmp$same_sig_at_05), nrow(cmp)))
if (any(!cmp$same_sig_at_05)) {
  d <- cmp[!cmp$same_sig_at_05, ]
  cat("- Coefficients whose significance differs:",
      paste(sprintf("%s / %s (p = %.3f vs %.3f)", d$outcome, d$term, d$p_value_q0, d$p_value_q1),
            collapse = "; "), "\n")
}
```

### 8.1 Diagnosis of the Change model under nAGQ = 1

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_nagq1
g7_q1 <- m1_list[[7]]
data.frame(method = c("nAGQ = 0", "nAGQ = 1"),
           sd_book     = c(attr(VarCorr(g7)$book_id, "stddev"), attr(VarCorr(g7_q1)$book_id, "stddev")),
           sd_reviewer = c(attr(VarCorr(g7)$reviewer_id, "stddev"), attr(VarCorr(g7_q1)$reviewer_id, "stddev")),
           intercept   = c(fixef(g7)[1], fixef(g7_q1)[1]),
           median_se_genre = c(median(sqrt(diag(vcov(g7)))[-1]), median(sqrt(diag(vcov(g7_q1)))[-1]))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_nagq1
ok6 <- cmp$outcome != "Change"
c(r_6_models = cor(cmp$log_odds_q0[ok6], cmp$log_odds_q1[ok6]),
  max_abs_diff_6_models = max(abs(cmp$diff_log_odds[ok6])),
  same_sig_6_models = sum(cmp$same_sig_at_05[ok6]), n_6_models = sum(ok6))
```

### 8.2 Conclusions of the robustness check

- **For six of the seven constructs the two methods agree almost perfectly.** The genre coefficients
  correlate at r > .999 within every one of these models, the largest difference is 0.18 on the log-odds
  scale, every sign is the same, and the random-effect SDs are similar (the Laplace fit gives slightly
  larger variances, most visibly for books in Absence of Naive Realism: SD 0.44 vs. 0.58).
- **Four borderline coefficients cross p = .05**, all from just above to just below:
  Fiction and Mystery / Thriller / Crime on Thought-Provoking (p = .064 → .028; .057 → .034),
  Romance on Critic (.099 → .034) and Poetry on Surprise (.059 → .047). None of the clearly
  significant effects changes. These four should be described as weak or borderline.
- **The nAGQ = 1 fit of Change is degenerate and should not be used.** Both random-intercept SDs
  explode to about 27 on the logit scale (vs. 0.94 and 0.54 with nAGQ = 0), the intercept moves from
  −3.0 to −30.9, and the genre standard errors inflate 20- to 50-fold, so no genre effect is significant
  and some odds ratios become absurd (e.g. Non-fiction OR = 355). This is a known failure of the Laplace
  approximation for **rare binary outcomes with many singleton clusters**: only 3% of reviews are coded
  Change = 1, and 32% of reviewers and 44% of books contribute a single review, so the approximate
  likelihood keeps "improving" as each positive review is absorbed into its own random effect. The higher
  log-likelihood of this fit (−5045 vs. −6285) is an artefact of the approximation, not a better model.
  The optimiser reports convergence only because it stopped, not because it found a valid estimate.
- **Recommendation:** report the nAGQ = 0 models as the main results (Sections 4–7), mention that the
  Laplace fits confirm them for six constructs, and treat the Change model's variance components with
  caution. If a stricter check for Change is needed, a model with a weakly informative prior on the
  random-effect variances (e.g. `blme::bglmer`), or a reviewer-only or book-only random intercept,
  would avoid the degenerate solution.
